features.rationale: kg's loader resolves against kg's own bounded load-path array and package state rather than Emacs' Lisp-visible load-path with .elc/.el/no-suffix probing, which is why the resolution half is kg-policy and lives in the load-path-search row. What IS Emacs-comparable is the value: since Phase 11 `load' answers t on success, as Emacs' does, where it answered nil before (11A Decision 5; load-returns-t pins it). There is no failure return to distinguish t from -- every way kg's load can fail raises, and since 11D Part 3 an enclosing condition-case can catch it (load-error-condition-reachability). The condition a missing file raises is Emacs' `file-missing' since Phase 12 (12D Part 2, the phase12-file-conditions row): it used to be a plain `error' whose message carried the path as prose, and the blocker Phase 11 recorded for it -- "condition subtypes with an inheritance test in fe's handler search" -- was stale when it was written, since fe has had that test since Phase 6. Since Phase 12's fix cycle `load' itself is prelude Lisp (lisp/prelude.el's loader section) over the C stream natives the loader-stream-natives row describes; resolution is unchanged and stays kg-policy.

Sub-plan 12D Part 2, and the item the Phase 12 fact audit found already half-built: `file-error' has been a row of fe's condition_parents[] since Phase 6 and has always been catchable from kg, so doc/TODO.md's claim that this needed "condition subtypes with an inheritance test in fe's handler search" was stale. `file-missing' under it is ONE DATA LINE (fe b030d0a), and it is what makes (signal 'file-missing ...) legal at all, since IsConditionSymbol gates `signal'. Exactly two kg sites raise it, both measured against Emacs 31.0.90 and both now byte-identical in class and data: the loader's cannot-open (src/lisp_io.c's read_whole_file) and `require' finding nothing in the load-path (src/lisp_require.c's resolve_require_path). The data is Emacs' uniform (OPERATION STRERROR PATH) triple of strings, with the FEATURE in the path slot for require, where nothing resolved. Everything else those two files raise is a kg-policy resource or limit error with no Emacs counterpart -- load depth, load-path full, out of memory, cyclic require, did-not-provide -- and stays a plain `error'. The loader's cannot-READ site also stays a plain `error', but NOT for lack of a counterpart: Emacs answers (file-error "Cannot open load file" "Is a directory" PATH) for (load DIRECTORY), measured on 31.0.90, so a (file-error ...) handler catches there and not here. Out of scope per 12A Decision 1, recorded so the next reader looks. TWO THINGS RECORDED RATHER THAN ASSERTED. (1) `permission-denied', Emacs' third file-error leaf: measurable only unprivileged, since chmod 000 is defeated by running as root, and this box runs the suite as root (12A Decision 1). kg raises the PARENT class, `file-error', for EACCES and nothing else, which is where a handler naming file-error catches it in either dialect. The split is on EACCES rather than on ENOENT because that was measured: a path whose parent is not a directory is ENOTDIR to kg's fopen and "No such file or directory" to Emacs, whose loader probes suffixes and answers its own not-found -- and it is file-missing on both sides (phase12-file-missing-not-a-directory). (2) The message. fe's `signal' uses the bare condition NAME as the completion message, so this change would have replaced kg's `cannot open PATH: No such file or directory' with the word `file-missing' and dropped the file name out of every diagnostic. render_file_condition() in src/lisp_core.c renders these two classes the way Emacs' error-message-string does instead -- `Cannot open load file: No such file or directory, /nope/x.el' -- rebuilt from the condition object rather than from state a raise would have to keep armed across a handler that catches it. The match is byte-for-byte for the (OPERATION STRERROR PATH) triple of strings -- the only shape kg's own raises produce -- including Emacs' rule that an empty OPERATION drops its `: ' separator; user-built shapes outside the triple (wrong arity, a non-string field) fall back to fe's own text by design. A general renderer for every condition is fe's `error-message' property, which neither tree has; this is the narrow version for the classes kg raises this way.

Recorded by sub-plan 10C (10A Decision 7 named it as an existing row; it was not one). Emacs' `load` searches `load-path`; kg's does not. Documented in README.md, doc/kg.1 and doc/lisp-api.md; the bounded array is a deliberate design (see src/lisp_require.c's header), not an unimplemented feature. Closed by Phase 11 sub-plan 11D Part 3 (11A Decision 5, Shape A); recorded by the Phase 10 acceptance review before that. Reader exhaustion was always catchable, being raised before the nested evaluator starts (test_exhaustion_catchability), and still is. PHASE 12 FIX-CYCLE CODA: the containment-and-resignal machinery this row describes was retired when `load' became a prelude read-eval loop in the caller's own run (see load-throw-reachability); the property now holds with no barrier at all -- an error inside a loaded form reaches an enclosing condition-case because nothing ever stood between them. The C half of the Phase 12 fix-cycle loader rebuild (sub-plan 12D Part 2, completed by the fix cycle on fe's FE_API_VERSION 8 input-unit trio). `load' and `require' are prelude Lisp loops; these natives own what C must own. internal--load-begin opens a load stream -- whole file into the next state.load_buffers slot, cursor and per-slot path copy beside it (fe borrows the unit label for the unit's whole lifetime), FeEnterInputUnit with the path as label -- and either returns a fully-open stream or raises with nothing changed, so the prelude's unwind-protect never sees partial state. internal--read-form answers the next form as the one-element list (FORM), keeping end-of-input (nil) distinguishable from a form reading as nil, with the form's own line latched so a raise while `eval'ing it reports path:LINE of the form. internal--load-end leaves the input unit and frees the buffer; it runs from the prelude loop's unwind-protect, i.e. on every completion kind via fe's cleanup drain. Handles are validated against the innermost open stream -- loads nest strictly, and a mismatched handle (or a user calling an internal-- native directly) is reported, not indexed with. internal--resolve-load is `load''s old name resolution unchanged. The require quartet: resolve (no-op arm, cycle and nesting verdicts, load-path resolution), push/pop (the cyclic-require stack, published inside the prelude unwind-protect and popped in its cleanup -- what used to be a C-side FeProtectWithCleanup), check (the did-not-provide verdict and the package-load perf accounting). kg-policy: Emacs has no such seam; what IS Emacs-comparable is the loader behaviour built on it, pinned by load-dynamic-extent and load-throw-reachability.

Both now ask lisp_io.c's lisp_has_el_suffix, the single copy of that question. test_require_el_suffix pins the fix and, deliberately, the three rules that did NOT move: a bare stem still gains .el, an absent file still fails naming what it looked for -- as Emacs' `file-missing' since Phase 12, where the message used to be kg's own 'cannot find in load-path' prose -- and the file the old code would have found, doubled.el.el, is unreachable with its marker unbound, and a FILENAME containing '/' is still literal -- neither suffixed nor searched. kg's `let' macro normalises its binding list and hands it to fe's core bindings-list `let'. Until Phase 11 it expanded to an immediate lambda application instead, which is why a `let' over a `defvar'd name was lexical: a lambda parameter is a lexical environment entry unconditionally, in fe and -- measured -- in Emacs 31 too, so the special flag is consulted at fe's binding-list paths and nowhere else (11A Decisions 2-3). The five dynamic cases here are the 11A grid's `let' half: nested extents (A3a), `setq' inside a binding writing the binding and not the value it hides (A2a), a closure reading the value in force when it is CALLED (A5), and the restore running on a throw (A6a) as well as on an error (A6b). The last two cases are guards, not targets: a defun parameter named after a special stays LEXICAL (A4), and a name no `defvar' ever named stays lexical under `let' (A13). An implementation that made every `let' dynamic would pass every target case here and fail both guards. The macro was not deleted outright, which 11D Part 2 proposed, because fe's core form raises wrong-type-argument for the one-element binding (a) where Emacs -- and kg before this change -- answers nil for (let ((a)) a); normalising in the macro keeps that, and keeps (let ((a 1 2)) a) answering 1, kg's long-standing reading of a shape Emacs rejects. One error class improved as a side effect and is recorded here because b975e79's shape table presents itself as complete and does not have it: (let (1) 5) raised invalid-function before the switch and raises wrong-type-argument after it, which is what the pinned Emacs 31.0.90 raises. Measured on both sides; no other shape in that table moved.

The capture/restore pair sub-plan 11D Part 4 replaced internal--save-excursion and internal--with-current-buffer with. Those two were natives that called the body as a thunk, which is what made a `throw' out of the body uncatchable outside the form; the two forms are now prelude macros over Lisp `unwind-protect' and only the editor state stays in C. (internal--excursion-capture SAVE-POINT) answers a right-gravity marker at point in the current buffer when SAVE-POINT is non-nil and the current buffer object when it is nil -- the two scopes save-excursion and with-current-buffer respectively preserve, which are the scopes the natives preserved before and Emacs' own. (internal--excursion-restore STATE) puts it back and releases it, tolerantly: a buffer killed underneath the form is a restore with nothing to restore to, not an error, because an unwind-protect cleanup that raises REPLACES the completion it was unwinding and would swallow the error that killed the buffer. The saved state is a GC-managed adapter object rather than a malloc'd record with an fe cleanup registration, so an unwind that never reaches the cleanup cannot leak one. kg-policy: Emacs has no such pair, and what IS Emacs-comparable is the behaviour of the two macros built on them.

A prelude macro over Lisp `unwind-protect' since sub-plan 11D Part 4, where it was a wrapper around the internal--save-excursion native before. The change of shape is what made a `throw' out of the body reach a `catch' outside the form (the catch-throw-reachability row); the state preserved is unchanged -- the current buffer and point in it, held by a right-gravity marker, so text inserted before the saved point carries it along. kg-policy because the state kg has to preserve is kg's; what is Emacs-comparable is the control flow through it, which the catch-throw-reachability and condition-case rows own. Two consequences of the macro shape are recorded rather than fixed, both found by the Phase 11 acceptance review. (1) The saved state is bound to the prelude temporary internal--excursion, so a body that ASSIGNS that name makes the cleanup raise -- and a raising cleanup replaces the completion it is unwinding (fe 06A Decision 4, which is Emacs' rule too), so the body's own error is lost: (condition-case e (save-excursion (setq internal--excursion nil) (error "MY-ERROR")) (error e)) answers the restore's type error, not MY-ERROR. It is the 11A Decision 3 capturable-temporaries exposure with a sharper consequence than the other 53 names, and doc/TODO.md carries it there. (2) The saved marker is an adapter pool object, so the restore RELEASES its record rather than waiting for the collector; without that the 65th save-excursion between two collections raised the pool's exhaustion error, which is what the review's blocker was. test_save_excursion_pool_bound and two PTY cases pin it. THE POOL IS NO LONGER WHAT BOUNDS NESTING. Sub-plan 12D Part 3 raised LISP_MAX_OBJECTS 64 -> 256 (12A Decision 5), which costs 88 bytes a record -- +16.5 KB of .bss, 332392 -> 349288 -- and zero scc, and the binding constraint on nested save-excursion became fe's evaluation frame limit instead: re-measured on the finished tree, 218 nested forms answer and the 219th raises `evaluation frame limit exceeded', which is the same 1095-frame arena partition `with-current-buffer' has always lived under (155 deep, 156 raising, unchanged). At 64 the 65th nested form raised. Emacs has no pool bound at all -- 200000 live markers and a million sequential excursions run, and its first ceiling is the C stack at about 50000 nested -- so this is kg narrower by design, three orders of magnitude closer than it was. COLLECTOR BACK-PRESSURE WAS MEASURED AND REJECTED rather than left unbuilt: at the nesting threshold every record is LIVE, so a forced full collection frees exactly zero and the next allocation still fails -- the audit proved it by bursting 40000 conses inside the 64th nested excursion -- and it would have cost a new fe entry point and a second pin move to fix a different bug (dropped garbage). A realloc'ing pool is ruled out by construction: records are addressed by pointer inside their FeTFex0 wrappers and kg registers no mark_fn, so nothing could fix the pointers up after a move. The marker mint's exhaustion message said "too many buffer objects" until the same slice; it says "too many marker objects" now, which is what every measurement of this bound actually prints.

A prelude macro over Lisp `unwind-protect' since sub-plan 11D Part 4, same change of shape as prelude-save-excursion above and for the same reason. It restores the current BUFFER and deliberately not point in it, which is Emacs' scope for the form -- it is save-current-buffer plus set-buffer -- and was the native's scope before. A buffer killed underneath the form is a restore with nothing to restore to rather than an error; see the native-excursion-capture-restore row for why a raising cleanup would be worse.

Closed by Phase 11 (11A Decisions 2-3); recorded as the manifest's sharpest divergence by sub-plan 10C before that. kg's `defvar' binds a value, leaves an already-bound name alone (first-defvar-wins, which the prelude-defvar case pins), and since Phase 11 also MARKS the symbol, which is what makes `let' over it dynamic. The two arities mark differently, and the difference is Emacs' measured one rather than a simplification: a two-argument `defvar' marks the symbol fully special (special-variable-p answers t -- phase11-dynamic-two-arg-defvar-special), while a one-argument `(defvar v)' sets the let-dynamic flag alone, so special-variable-p answers nil (phase11-dynamic-one-arg-defvar-not-special) and yet `(let ((v 5)) (f))' is 5 -- which is where the first approximation below is measured, in the separate row phase11-one-arg-defvar-file-scope. Binding is shallow: the binding swaps the global value cell and records the old contents -- or the fact that there were none, which is why phase11-dynamic-let-over-unbound-special sees boundp go nil again afterwards -- and the restore runs on every completion kind fe has. The headline the phase exists for is phase11-dynamic-temporary-setting-idiom: the ordinary Emacs temporary-setting idiom, written over three top-level forms, answered nil here and t in Emacs, silently. TWO RESIDUALS ARE RECORDED RATHER THAN DEFENDED (rewritten at the Phase 12 fix cycle: the paragraph here used to record the pre-Phase-12 GLOBAL marking, and in the wrong direction). First, since fe 38caa63 a one-argument mark is scoped to its INPUT UNIT -- one `load', `require', batch file, M-: or prelude install, NOT per file as shorthand sometimes has it: two loads of the same file are two units -- and the measured residuals are (a) NARROWER than Emacs: a `defun' written after the defvar in file A stays dynamic in Emacs when called from file B, where kg, consulting the flag where the `let' runs, answers lexically; and (b) a widening: in host context (input_scope 0 -- hooks, command dispatch, process callbacks, any FeCall from C) every mark is visible. fe's one-arg-defvar-scope-carrier row carries the probe grid and the unwind guarantee; phase11-one-arg-defvar-file-scope pins what the oracle shim's per-form scoping asks, and test_phase12_one_arg_defvar_file_scope is the two-file probe agreeing with Emacs byte-for-byte. Second, the 53 generically-named `internal--let' temporaries in lisp/prelude.el (result, res, doc, name, ...) become dynamically capturable the moment a user `defvar's such a name -- which is exactly Emacs' own exposure for lexical-binding libraries, so it is recorded, not defended (11A Decision 3). Two of kg's then-recorded silent divergences were deliberately NOT made load-bearing in the pure file, which is what makes the agreement a property rather than a coincidence: nothing rebinds a defvar'd variable around a call (prelude-defvar), and no returned value contains a (quote X) form (writer-quote-abbreviation). Phase 15's regex-from-Lisp seam. The engine is src/regex.h's, already behind C-s and re-search-forward; what string-match adds is a string subject and Emacs' character-indexed match data, converted from the engine's byte spans where the subject is still in hand. Two properties of that engine are inherited rather than papered over, and the second case pins both: `^' and `$' anchor the whole subject rather than each line of it (kg's buffer search hands the engine one row at a time and so never needed a line anchor), and matching is case-SENSITIVE, where Emacs consults case-fold-search, whose default is t. Phase 15. The escaped set is Emacs 31.0.90's own, measured character by character: `.', `*', `+', `?', `[', `^', `$' and backslash, and NOT `]' -- a `]' outside a bracket expression is an ordinary character in this dialect. The case reports codepoints rather than the string itself because fe's writer does not re-escape a backslash inside a printed string and Emacs' prin1 does (doc/lisp-api.md's differences section); comparing the characters compares the answer rather than the two printers.

Emacs' (match-string N) with no STRING after a *string* match reads the current buffer and is args-out-of-range there; kg reads its buffer too, so neither side answers anything useful and the case does not ask.

Emacs' SPEC syntax minus the named character classes: `[:alpha:]' and its family are read as the ordinary characters they are made of. Everything else is measured against 31.0.90 and agrees -- a leading `^' negates (so "" skips nothing and "^" skips everything), `-' between two characters is a range, a backslash quotes the next character, and the comparison is over CODEPOINTS rather than bytes, so a spec naming a multi-byte character skips whole glyphs. A class table populated with a guess would be worse than a missing one, so the gap is recorded here instead. The set is bounded at 64 ranges and a longer spec raises rather than truncating.
The backward half of native-skip-chars-forward, sharing its parser and therefore its recorded gap: named character classes are not understood. The distance it answers is negative, as Emacs'.

One edit-gateway call, so one undo step, exactly as native-insert and native-delete-region are. The divergence is at the ends of the buffer: Emacs signals `end-of-buffer'/`beginning-of-buffer' and deletes nothing, where kg clamps the count and deletes what is there. Same cause as native-forward-char's -- fe's condition table holds neither name -- and the same doc/TODO.md row covers it, but the consequence is larger here, since a clamped delete loses text an Emacs user would still have.

Answers nil for a buffer that visits no file, as Emacs does, and that half is comparable (phase17-with-temp-buffer and phase17-buffer-modified-p both ask it). What is not comparable, and is the divergence, is the value for a buffer that DOES visit one: Emacs stores an absolute path, kg stores the name as the command line or C-x C-f gave it, because kg has no expand-file-name to build an absolute one with and inventing a directory would be worse than reporting what the editor holds. The question it asks internally is buf_visits_file()'s, not `is the name field set': kg keeps a C-x b buffer's NAME in the same field, and such a buffer visits nothing.

A prelude macro over get-buffer-create + with-current-buffer + unwind-protect + kill-buffer, as the plan specifies. Three details are kg's and each is forced, and none of them is observable as a value: the buffer's NAME carries a gensym suffix, because kg has no generate-new-buffer and a fixed name would make a nested use reuse the buffer it is already inside; the cleanup clears the modified flag first, because kg's kill-buffer refuses a modified buffer rather than asking; and the kill is wrapped in ignore-errors, because a cleanup that raises REPLACES the completion it is unwinding, which would lose the body's value. That last one has a measurable bound: kg refuses a kill when the editor's lifecycle event queue is full, the queue drains once per keystroke, and each temp buffer costs three of its 64 slots -- so one command that opens more than about twenty temp buffers starts leaking them rather than failing.

`(goto-char (point-min))' and nothing more, which is the Emacs manual's own advice for Lisp code. Emacs' beginning-of-buffer is a COMMAND and pushes the mark, so C-x C-x returns you; kg's does not, because kg's set-mark also lights the region up -- a Lisp call has no business doing that -- and kg has no unhighlighted push-mark to use instead. Point lands in the same place, which phase17-buffer-ends pins.
